item.title: Jam update: Sun 11:16 PM
item.description: Sunday, 11:30 PM: the co-owner's day, in seven short stories.
item.content:encoded:
Jam update: Sun 11:16 PM

Sunday, November 15, 2026 at 11:16 PM Central

Sunday, 11:30 PM: the co-owner's day, in seven short stories

The jam is over and the game is in. Before we close the day, here is what came out of one person's afternoon of testing: the co-owner, who owns the art and UI look and tested every menu on an Xbox this weekend, from the pad, in plain words, usually within a minute of a new build. Same labels as always: PLAYED means someone ran it in a game session; BUILT means it compiles and was read by a second person, but nobody has seen it work. The quotes are the co-owner's own words from the day.

  • The button picture that could not be drawn. The TALK TO button fires on the pad's A press, and the co-owner wanted the button to say so: "a is fine for the talk, just should say it." Epic's UI library can draw a key picture for any input action, so the plan was to point one at the action that draws A. Three attempts later we had a rule instead of a picture. One action draws the wrong button (Y, not A) on an Xbox pad. Four others draw nothing, because they never reach a player and Epic's own check rejects them with a box that names nothing. One is legal and draws a blank. And a picture hidden in the editor re-shows itself while the game runs. In the end the buttons that fire on A carry no picture at all, because no stock asset draws the right one. A real A picture of our own, swapped by the player's device, is on the list for next time. BUILT.
  • The white frame on the Set page. On the Set and Genre page the white focus frame vanished the moment a card was picked. It was not gone: the gold SELECTED frame and the white one sat in the same card, gold drawn on top. The fix was six small moves in the card's layer order, with both frames kept under the button so no press could be eaten. Someone walked every card on a pad: white stays over gold on the picked card, and the D-pad and A work on all six. PLAYED on a pad.
  • READY TO DIRECT, twice, to the co-owner's spec. The spec is three full-size renders and a palette note: a hotter golden sunburst, a gold ticket, gold pedestals, purple accents only, a green START and a blue EDIT. The first pass fixed a solid white hover box, a stretched purple cost plate and a floating portrait. The co-owner's verdict on the console was a precise fix list: "the studio cash portion looks like it might be the same color as the background ... two versions of yellow on top of each other", "The camera's wording is not inside the box. The FunkOps is not inside the box. Either take the box out or make the words fit". The second pass took the box out, made the cash line black with a white outline, put the actor labels on the drum faces, moved the titles onto their plates and made the banner taller. The co-owner's answer: "ok this play is good". PLAYED.
  • A power cut and a squeal. At 5:59 PM the power went out. The editor came back at 6:02 with no project, the files were synced to the latest in the gap before the map loaded (the only safe moment to sync widgets), and a build was pushed at 6:16. Then: "there is a hard to listen to high-pitched squeal that makes me and my pcs shudder". A spectrogram of the capture showed one steady 12 kHz line from the first second of the menus, and none in an earlier capture, so it was not the take, not the music and not the co-owner's ears. Our first theory was a feedback loop in the voice rooms after a change that landed in between. One test ended the hunt: "going back to the lobby to check if sound stops. it does not. xbox is going off." The console had come back from the power cut in a bad audio state. A power cycle and an HDMI reset fixed it: "That works now." The squeal was not in the game.
  • The menu that fell off the screen. "ui is off the screen on the directors call now. i dont know what changed." What changed was the WRAP / CARRY ON row landing inside the menu's vertical stack. After a CUT it appears, grows the stack by about a hundred pixels and pushes RETAKE and SETTINGS off the bottom. The row now sits in its own slot above the panel, and the money pop-ups moved to the top right from a mock-up the co-owner drew. BUILT.
  • Hot Set, in the title and on the wrap sheet. At 7:10 PM: "Rename the project to Hot Set." The project's title was changed and read back from the running editor, and the final version carries it. At 7:30 PM the co-owner delivered a new end card because the wrap sheet still said DIRECTOR'S CUT. The delivered pictures had sample numbers and buttons baked in, so only the banner region was placed onto the real background; the live numbers and buttons are code and were not touched. BUILT.
  • The trailer and the key art. The co-owner cut a trailer in two versions, with a no-music cut and review stills, and drew the key art: a sunset director's chair, a comic-brush logo and a tall "ACTION OR GO HOME" poster.

NOT seen yet: the A button picture of our own, the final build on a console after the last change, and a second person joining the final version.

item.title: Jam update: Sun 8:07 PM

item.content:encoded:
Jam update: Sun 8:07 PM

Sunday, November 15, 2026 at 8:07 PM Central

Sunday, 8:30 PM: the clock has run out, and this is where the game stands

The jam deadline has just passed. Same labels as always: PLAYED means someone ran it in a game session; BUILT means it compiles and was read by a second person, but nobody has seen it work.

Submitted. The owners confirmed that the jam form went in before the 7:59 PM deadline. The entry is the team's version 1 of the project, now titled Hot Set, with a gameplay video. We are not going to say how it will do; we have not seen it as a stranger would.

Play it and rate it on the game page (https://bizanator.itch.io/hot-set) and the jam entry page (https://itch.io/jam/2026-epic-ai-megajam/rate/5377098).

Music: PLAYED. The menu and office music was silent for most of the afternoon. It is in the final build, and both the owner and the co-owner have heard it in a session.

The final stretch, in the order we met it.

  • READY TO DIRECT and the pay pop-ups: PLAYED (see below).
  • Actors taking direction: PLAYED, with a catch. A fix made the final build: the owner played it and the actors kept the notes ("Yes, Director"). They still miss some notes, so it is not every time.
  • Guest Star and the voice fix: PLAYED earlier today. A surprise actor walks on mid-take, and every actor is heard after a TALK.
  • Settings, HEAD TO SET and the How to Play card: BUILT. They compile and were read by a second person. Nobody has pressed them on a controller since the last change.

What the co-owner built and drove, that players see.

  • READY TO DIRECT, to the co-owner's look. The co-owner's spec was a hotter golden sunburst, a gold ticket, gold pedestals, purple accents only, a green START and a blue EDIT. The first pass fixed a solid white hover box, a stretched cost plate and a floating portrait; the pad test then asked for the cash line to stand out from the background and the camera and actor wording to sit inside their boxes. The second pass took the box out, put the cash line in black with a white outline, put the actor labels on the drum faces and made the banner taller. PLAYED.
  • Pay pop-ups, top right. The money that pops up as lines land moved to the top right of the screen, from a mock-up the co-owner drew. PLAYED.
  • Hot Set, in the title and on the wrap sheet. The project is now titled Hot Set, and a new end card replaced the old DIRECTOR'S CUT banner on the wrap sheet. Only the banner was replaced; the live numbers and buttons are code and were not touched. BUILT.
  • The team upload. The final build was uploaded from the co-owner's side as the team's version 1 of Hot Set.
  • A dock fix, also from the co-owner's pad test: PLAYED. After a CUT, the WRAP / CARRY ON row on the Director's Call menu pushed RETAKE and SETTINGS off the bottom of the screen. The row now sits in its own slot above the panel, and the footer stays on screen.

What we did not get to. The anime look is off in this build. The new interface sounds are not in. Nothing has been joined or saved by anyone other than the co-owner's own account, so how the game behaves for a second person is NOT seen.

NOT seen yet: the game as a stranger would meet it, a second person joining the final version, the interface sounds, the anime look, the Settings and HEAD TO SET buttons on a controller after the last change, and anything on the cinematic branch that was not switched on. Thank you for following along. If there is another entry, it will say what happened after the deadline.

Jam update: Sun 4:28 PM

Sunday, November 15, 2026 at 4:28 PM Central

Sunday, 4:30 PM: a guest star walks on, voices fixed, and the last build is close

Three and a half hours to the deadline. Same labels as always: PLAYED means someone ran it in a game session; BUILT means it compiles and was read by a second person, but nobody has seen it work.

Guest Star: a surprise actor walks onto the set. Mid-take, a quick-time prompt can bring on a guest, and landing it earns a cash bonus. The guest stays for the rest of the episode and leaves when a new show starts. PLAYED by the owner: on a retake the guest kept the same slot and mark with no respawn flicker, spoke their lines, and the log shows the slot freed again on a new show. The guest now has a picture on the "GUEST STAR!" card that pops up when they walk on. That picture is BUILT; nobody has looked at it on screen yet.

Quick-time prompts, made fairer. A wrong key that was already in flight used to end the prompt almost instantly (46 milliseconds in one log). The fix adds half a second of grace, and the button picture is bigger. Both are BUILT. Nobody has played the new timing, so we cannot say yet whether half a second feels right.

Voices: every actor heard after a TALK. After talking to one actor between takes, the next take could play only that one actor's voice. The fix rebuilds the stage voice channel after each TALK and resets the talk target. Along with one placed-setting change, it is in the game now. PLAYED: the owner tried it on the console and reported that the voice fix worked, and the log shows the rebuild after TALK. What we still do not know is whether an actor remembers the direction they were given after the rebuild. That check is open.

Space Station alarm, once per take. The alarm is now a single 10-second moment per take instead of a constant. An earlier test showed the red beacon and red room lingering long after the alarm was logged off; after the fix, a check saw no alarm and no red room at the start of a take. The owner also played the Space Station and said it works. The fix is BUILT; the alarm's 10 seconds have not been timed by eye.

The Set and Genre screen, plus six new genre cards. The co-owner's new Set and Genre screen was PLAYED: every press was heard, and backing out and re-entering was clean three times. A focus fix, so the picked card stays white over gold and the D-pad and A work on every card, is being finished. It is not in the game yet, it waits for a controller check, and it may miss this build. Six new genre cards (Western, Film Noir, Drama, Horror, Comedy, Sci-Fi) are in the game, each checked as an image. Nobody has seen them in a take.

A Settings sheet, a slot row, and HEAD TO SET. The Settings sheet has switches for events, goals and guest stars. The slot row is a button on the Director's Call menu that offers WRAP (bank the take) or CARRY ON between takes, and in the office it becomes HEAD TO SET, which sends the player to the set. All of it landed and is BUILT. It still needs a controller pass, so the button glyphs on it are hidden for now.

How to Play card. A short how-to appears beside the Showrunner while the player talks in the office and goes away when the talk ends. It landed and is BUILT; it has not yet shown up in a live session.

Honest open items. Actors still do not always take direction. The fix is being worked on and is not in the game. The anime look and the new interface sounds are next build, if at all.

NOT seen yet: a published copy of the game, the Guest Star card picture, the new quick-time timing, the Space Station alarm's 10 seconds timed by eye, the Set and Genre focus fix (not in the game yet), the Settings sheet and HEAD TO SET, the How to Play card, actors taking direction, and everything on the cinematic branch (title, credits, office, unlock card, hints). Next entry about 8:30 PM, after the deadline, as a wrap-up if there is anything to say.

Jam update: Sun 11:42 AM

Sunday, November 15, 2026 at 11:42 AM Central

Sunday, 12:30 PM: two-shots in frame, a seventh actor in test, and a lot of small fixes waiting for a play

Seven and a half hours to the deadline. Same labels as always: PLAYED means someone ran it in a game session; BUILT means it compiles and was read by a second person, but nobody has seen it work.

Played by the owner this morning. A third session on the test copy: a dust-storm prompt and a second one on the next take, both tapped through; the goal that carries over to the next take (it was kept, then met on take two); and the PROPS button switching tabs with one press. Take two ended with five stars. PLAYED. Two things we cannot know without asking: why two of three TALK presses closed straight away, and what a mid-take shoulder-button press was meant to do.

Two-shots, part two. After the cameras stopped blocking themselves, the next problem was where the actors landed in the frame. The first framing pass (version 2) has landed and was PLAYED: both actors are now balanced in the shot instead of one at the edge. A third pass (version 3) pulls both actors' faces clear of the on-screen buttons, which cover the left and right sides of the picture. It is BUILT, compile-checked, read by a second person, and sits in the owner's test copy waiting to be seen.

Peely, a seventh actor: in test. The menu now shows a second Casting Call page, and the character, the Director's cast slot and the persona text are all built. The first full test found a real fault: the second page cannot be reached with the controller's shoulder buttons or the keyboard. Focus only moves to the first card, so a player could never pick the seventh actor. BROKEN in test; it is being traced now. Nobody has seen Peely standing on a set yet.

Reward sounds are coming back. The tick of the money counter, the thud and the level-up chime went silent when the sound route changed. A fix that plays them through placed audio players is BUILT, compiled, and read by two people. We checked from the saved level data that nothing needs to be ticked by hand for it to work. Nobody has heard it yet.

Prop jitter. Props handed to an actor were colliding with the actor and bouncing. A fix that makes held props never collide is BUILT and compile-checked, and a test take that counts the bounces is running.

Two more, re-made on the latest code. A lighter haze over the studio sky, and an early-press fix for the quick-time prompts, so a press before the prompt is ignored and only a missed prompt counts as a miss. Both are BUILT and compile-checked, and both wait for the owner's approval card. They are NOT in the game yet.

New rule for Verse changes. Every code change now gets its own card with the exact lines, for the owner to approve before it lands. It is slower but it means nothing changes without being seen.

NOT seen yet: a published copy of the game, the version-3 framing, Peely on a set, the reward sounds, the prop fix, the haze, the early-press fix, and everything on the cinematic branch. Next entry about 4:30 PM.

The art team spent the latest stretch working on props and materials, giving the island's look a bit more polish. There's no big headline news to share right now, but steady progress is being made behind the scenes. With about eight hours left in the jam, we're pushing to bring everything together, so stay tuned for more updates soon!

Jam update: Sun 8:12 AM

Sunday, November 15, 2026 at 8:12 AM Central

Sunday, 8:30 AM: the two-shot never worked, and now we know why

Eleven and a half hours to the deadline. Same labels as always: PLAYED means someone ran it in a game session; BUILT means it compiles and was read by a second person, but nobody has seen it work.

The big find: two-actor shots have essentially never worked in a live game. The Director is meant to cut to a shot with both actors in it. In every take we looked at overnight, including the owner's own takes from Saturday, it refused and fell back to a close-up or the wide: about 400 refusals, none clear at full distance. We tested our guesses one at a time and then proved the cause in the editor: our own parked close-up cameras, and sometimes a held prop, sat on the line the camera uses to check that it can see the actor. The camera was being blocked by our own equipment. The fix, which tells that check to ignore those objects, is BUILT and compile-checked. The first test take is encouraging: on the Theatre set a two-shot played with no fallback, and the log has no blocked lines at all. That is one take on one set, so it is PLAYED once, not proven. The rest of the test run (more sets, framing judged by eye) is under way. A second change then keeps both actors' faces clear of the on-screen buttons. It is BUILT and compile-checked; nobody has seen it yet.

Standing marks on eight sets: landed and played. On eight of the twelve sets the second actor used to stand 8 to 18 metres from the first. The new marks put them 2.5 to 3.8 metres apart, side by side. They are now on the overnight branch. PLAYED: on the Wild West set the two-shot plays for the first time, with both actors in the frame, and nobody floats or clips. On the Theatre, Jungle Temple and Dock sets the shot still fell back to a close-up, which is the camera problem above, not the marks. Our art reviewer judged the frames green. Two sets had a tie between two spots, and the test run showed it, so each was moved by 10 centimetres. Those two fixes are BUILT, not seen.

Held props: half landed. What landed and was PLAYED: one prop per actor, a thrown-in prop stays for retakes and drops on a cast swap, and a seated actor holds it at chest height. What is still wrong, also PLAYED: one-handed props sit about 10 centimetres in front of the hand, and two-handed props float, because gesture animations override the grip. The fix is BUILT and being tested now.

One set's lights were on everywhere: fixed, pending one frame. The four space-station lights are now switched off on every other set. Castle and Haunted Manor look the same before and after, which is what we wanted. BUILT. It still needs a frame showing the lights come on in the Space Station itself.

The menu highlight: three options for the co-owner. The current look, a stronger one and a gold one are all built. The gold is clearly the easiest to see, and it follows the real focus (we checked keyboard-then-controller and it never stays on the wrong button). Notes on the card: white text on gold is soft, and one plate is already yellow at rest. PLAYED, waiting on the co-owner's pick.

A seventh actor. A candidate for the new Casting Call card is an in-engine render framed like the six. The character still needs one proper spawn test: our first attempt used the wrong method, so it proves nothing either way. NOT seen.

NOT seen yet: a published copy of the game, the mouse path played by a person, the two-shot fix across all sets, the prop fix, the Space Station lights, the anime look in a real take, and everything on the cinematic branch (title, credits, office, unlock card, hints). Next entry about 12:30 PM.

Quiet stretch on the island right now, but we've got a fresh screenshot to show for it and the build is holding steady. With about 11 hours left in the jam, we're lining up the next round of work and can't wait to share more. Stay tuned for new looks at the island soon!

Highlights

Jam update: Sun 4:29 AM

Sunday, November 15, 2026 at 4:29 AM Central

Sunday, 4:30 AM: three fixes played, three finds, and a pile of polish nobody has played yet

Same rule as always: PLAYED means someone ran it in a game session; BUILT means it compiles and was read by a second pair of eyes but nobody has seen it work. Fifteen hours to the deadline.

Played and fixed

  • The results sheet and the take bar. The results sheet used to close itself after 12 seconds when opened with the mouse. It now stays up, tested with the mouse and a virtual controller (it stayed past 15 seconds both times; on the controller it ran to the 60-second safety timer). The take bar's line counter, goal, CUT and camera buttons now sit in their own bands on a small screen. PLAYED. It is on the overnight branch only. A real console controller has not tried it.
  • The Director's Call menu, controller focus. Before, after using the keyboard, the next controller press could fire TALK by mistake. A small guard now ignores the first press after focus comes back. We ran all five steps (keyboard then controller, controller note, mouse click, results after keyboard) and all five passed. PLAYED. It still waits for the co-owner's OK on the look of the highlight before it goes anywhere.
  • The "THAT'S A WRAP" card. It shows on a natural last line, and CUT during the card goes cleanly to the results. PLAYED in the Castle.

Three live problems found, all being fixed

  • Held props float. A rose bouquet hung 20 to 30 cm in front of and above the hand. We saw it on the test machine and the lead confirmed it on the frame. The new hold position and prop table are BUILT and read; they have not been played yet. They are the next test run.
  • Two-shots blocked on eight sets. On eight of twelve sets the two actors were placed 8 to 18 metres apart, too far for one shot, so the camera fell back to a close-up or the wide (the owner's own log from last night shows it on the Western set). New standing marks put them 2.5 to 3.8 metres apart, side by side. They are shelved for all eight sets; each point was checked twice by two people, from the placed data (floor height, clear space, angle to the camera). BUILT; nobody has seen the new shots. Two spots (Haunted Manor, Theatre) were moved on the second check because the first points were weak.
  • One set's lights are on everywhere. Four space-station lights were never switched off, so they lit the Theatre, the Haunted Manor, the Diner and the Castle too. Every frame we had of those sets showed that orange and blue wash. The fix registers the lights with the set so they only come on in space. BUILT. We still need a before-and-after pair on a dark interior to make sure nothing goes flat.

Anime look. The flat side-on camera twins are built and read. The test plan uses the three sets with the best angles (Diner, Wild West, Space Station); Jungle Temple and Haunted Manor stay out of it for now. BUILT, not seen. We also have a stronger focus highlight for the menu as a second option, waiting for the co-owner's pick.

The cinematic branch. A title sequence with the HOT SET logo, end credits, a camera push into the Showrunner's office, a level-unlock card and three tutorial hints are all on a separate branch, each behind its own switch, all OFF. BUILT and read; never played. The first attempt to play the title failed four times because the test machine would not launch a second game session. Nothing from this branch is in the game we would submit.

Also being built: a seventh actor, a banana-costume character, as a cast member. Character, persona text and menu are in place or shelved; the spawn is not yet proven.

NOT seen yet: a published copy of the game, the mouse path played by a person, the new camera marks, the light fix, the prop fix, the weather card (blocked by missing level data), and anything on the cinematic branch.

Next entry around 8:30 AM.

Things are quiet on the island front this morning, but we're keeping the momentum going. The team is tidying up and lining everything up for the next big push, and we've got fresh screenshots to share with you. With about 15 hours left in the jam, we're settling in for the final stretch and can't wait to show you more soon.

Highlights

In progress

  • Maintain overnight run evidence ledger for the 2026-11-15 morning report

Jam update: Sun 12:34 AM

Sunday, November 15, 2026 at 12:34 AM Central

Sunday, 12:30 AM: where the game really stands

An honest read of the whole build, written at half past midnight with about 16 and a half hours to the code freeze (5:00 PM) and about 19 and a half to the submission (7:59 PM), all times Central. Every line carries one label: PLAYED (a person saw it work), IN TEST, BUILT (written and compiled, not seen), BROKEN, NOT STARTED, or NOT VERIFIED. "The snapshot" is the labelled copy of the code taken at 12:15 AM; overnight work goes on a separate branch.

1. The build

  • Compiles at the snapshot: BUILT. 0 errors and 0 warnings in the editor around midnight, and a fresh-editor build at 12:04 AM said success.
  • Launches: the last test sessions ran at 11:12 PM, 11:21 PM (the owner's last take) and 11:34 PM. The exact snapshot has not been launched yet.
  • Engine validation: on the overnight branch, 5,089 objects valid, 0 invalid, 0 not validated (about 12:20 AM). Not measured on the snapshot alone.
  • A published copy of the game: NOT STARTED. Nobody has played one.

2. The take, on a controller unless stated

  • Lobby to Casting Call: PLAYED (an Xbox pad at about 10:53 PM after a hotfix, "good now"; the owner's PlayStation 9:44 to 10:15 PM).
  • Set and Genre, the yellow page: PLAYED (the owner, 10:42 PM). The new widget screen is switched off.
  • Interview by voice: PLAYED (the owner's microphone, 10:42 to 10:43 PM, four talk cycles). The held-button plate is a review copy, not in the snapshot.
  • Interview to automatic show start: PLAYED.
  • Take rolls, cameras, captions: PLAYED (the owner, 11:04 to 11:08 PM, four takes).
  • LINE and GOAL on the take bar: BROKEN. The text overlaps the CUT and camera labels. Fix BUILT, not run.
  • CUT to results, and "take too short": PLAYED (the owner, about 10:20 PM).
  • A take that ends by itself, to the results offer and the sheet: PLAYED (the owner's PlayStation 11:07 to 11:08 PM; the Xbox pad).
  • Results sheet: BROKEN. A sheet opened by a press closes itself after 12 seconds. Fix BUILT, not run.
  • NEXT EPISODE, NEW SHOW, SUBMIT CUT: PLAYED.
  • Props on the left bumper: BUILT, not run on a pad.
  • A seated actor: BROKEN / IN TEST. The 3-second flicker was seen at 9:54 PM; the one-play fix is log-only so far; a 30-second idle check is running.
  • Seated gestures: BROKEN. The actor rises at a seated Point (11:21 PM); parked, not in the snapshot.
  • Mouse, by a person: NOT VERIFIED.
  • No microphone: PLAYED (a test machine took the no-microphone route, 11:14 to 11:18 PM; an 8-line take ran).

3. Content

  • Sets: Diner PLAYED (11:16 to 11:21 PM); Wild West PLAYED, with the seated actor standing on the chair (BROKEN, fix BUILT); Jungle Temple PLAYED; Castle PLAYED; Space Station PLAYED, with an orange Western sky (BROKEN look, fix BUILT). Theatre, Dock, Sound Stage, Farm, Beach, Haunted Manor: NOT VERIFIED tonight.
  • Genres: Drama, Western, Film Noir, Horror PLAYED; Comedy and Sci-Fi NOT VERIFIED tonight.
  • Actors: Jonesy, Eternal Knight, Ghoul PLAYED; Meow Skulls PLAYED (through a lock hole that is now fixed); Rabbit Raider and Funk Ops NOT VERIFIED.
  • Music beds: BUILT; the licence terms of two AI music tools are still open.
  • Props: BROKEN (oversized placed props were handed out); fix BUILT.

4. Known issues

  • Hold-to-talk reaching the Showrunner: PLAYED.
  • Debug text: the frame-rate block in our frames is Fortnite's own overlay; none of ours is known. NOT VERIFIED on a fresh frame.
  • Controller focus on the Director's Call menu: presses PLAYED; the visible highlight BROKEN (not obvious).
  • Floating stage-light housings: PLAYED hidden.
  • HOW TO PLAY card: NOT IN THE SNAPSHOT.
  • Noir fog: NOT IN THE SNAPSHOT. Space Station look: BUILT, not seen. Face lighting: no change tonight. Blocked shots: BUILT, not seen (the fault was seen in the owner's film).
  • Score screen: PLAYED; after a retake from a line the numbers did not add up; fix BUILT.

5. Ship blockers (things that stop a judge finishing one take)

  • A published copy has never been played. About 1 hour: the co-owner publishes, QA plays.
  • The mouse path has never been played by a person. About half an hour.
  • The results sheet closes itself after 12 seconds. About half an hour plus a pad run; fix BUILT.

No step is known to be BROKEN in a way that stops a controller take at the snapshot.

6. Cut candidates (not needed for one clean take)

Hazard prompts (off) and the button-picture fix, 1 hour. Seated gestures (parked), 3 hours. Guest stars, NOT STARTED, 4 hours. The Showrunner offering sets by voice (off), 1 hour. A settings sheet, 1.5 hours. The new Set and Genre screen, 1 hour. The READY TO DIRECT kit screen (held), 1.5 hours. CUT-opens-menu on, 1.5 hours. Camera styles and flat-camera twins, 2 hours. A cinematic branch, NOT STARTED, 4 hours and more. An event scheduler, NOT STARTED, 3 hours.

7. Submission

  • Trailer: BUILT as a draft, 44.8 seconds with game sound. The owner has not listened yet, and the title and end cards await the co-owner.
  • Store page: NOT STARTED; a human presses submit.
  • Pre-jam assets and AI tools declaration: a draft exists and two items are open: where one menu came from, and the music licences.
  • Devlog: live.

8. What changed since Saturday 1:30 AM

Cameras are smoother ("a lot smoother", the owner). Seats got floor-level marks, a seated start and a landing check. The sit loop is now one long play. The story data moved into six per-genre files. Weather has a twist, a card and a storm prompt. Hazard prompts exist (now off) with a rule for a miss. Pads get a results offer on the menu. The Xbox menu was fixed and the yellow Set page kept. Talk has a hold-to-talk pill. CUT can open the menu (switch off), and the ending has a soft beat. Goals are kept across a CUT (overnight branch only). Locked actors are refused by voice. Props have one-button access and a genre offer. A snapshot and an overnight branch were made.

9. Unknowns

The exact snapshot launched as a build; validation on the snapshot alone; how a published build behaves (the Showrunner and actors, saves, notes); the mouse; five sets and two actors not seen tonight; whether any debug text of ours shows; hand-prop size, the lock fallback and the indoor sky have no verdict from play.

Sections 2 and 5 will be re-posted when the running tests finish.

The team is taking a short breather with no big new updates to share right now, but the island is still moving along. With about 19 hours left in the jam, there's plenty of time for fresh progress to land. Stay tuned for the next look at what's coming together.

item.content:encoded:
Jam update: Sun 12:29 AM

Sunday, November 15, 2026 at 12:29 AM Central

Saturday night: the director takes the chair

Until tonight, every take we could point to had been run by a test machine or by us. Tonight the owner played on their own console, with a controller and a microphone. Three things got a pass.

  • The hold-to-talk prompt. While you talk to the Showrunner, a small plate shows the real talk button for your controller, lights up while it is held, and counts the time left. The owner tried it with a real microphone: pass.
  • The weather picture card. A twist in the weather now shows a card on screen. It passed, with a catch: at 11:09 PM the owner decided the rule behind it made no sense (cutting the scene should never cost you money), so the card now belongs to a new "storm coming" prompt that is built and not yet seen.
  • Locked actors, refused in character. Asking the Showrunner for an actor you have not unlocked now gets a polite no, with the price. A hole that let a locked actor be cast for free through her is closed. Pass.

A flicker found on the owner's own recording. A seated actor kept snapping to standing for an instant. Frame by frame, it came every three seconds, the length of the seated clip, so the spacing fits the loop restarting. Our first fix did not cure it, and we said so. The next one plays the seat clip once as a long loop; its log looks right, but we have no clean picture of it yet. Also found: the actor's boots sat on the chair, not the floor. Seated gestures made the actor stand up, so they are parked.

Screens that went deaf on a pad. The new Set screen ignored the owner's PlayStation pad after its first highlight, and a back button trapped another pad's casting page. A layering fault turned up by putting two versions side by side. Until the new screen is seen alive on a PlayStation, the game keeps the older one. New rule: no input change goes in without a run on a pad.

CUT keeping the scene open, and a softer ending. The ending, a short hold on the wide shot after the last line, was played and seen. The part where CUT keeps the take open for notes, retake or wrap is built behind a switch that is off until it is proven.

An honest verdict from outside. The co-owner's playtester tried the falling-light and "press as it closes" moments and said they took away from the story and broke the immersion. The button picture was also too small to read. The owner's answer: add a settings option to disable events, goals and guest stars. Hazard prompts are off for the private-code test.

The snapshot. At a quarter past midnight the code was snapshotted, labelled and kept as it stands, and a separate branch was opened from it for the overnight work, so the safe copy stays safe.

Not seen yet: the storm prompt, a goal carried across a cut, the new chairs with an actor on them, and a clean seated take. A first cut of the submission video, with game sound, exists as a draft the owner has not heard. All money in the game is in-game cash.

The jam is in full swing and we're keeping things under wraps for the moment, with no big news to share just yet. The team is heads-down building, and there are still about 19 hours left on the clock. Check back soon, because we'll have fresh updates and a first look at the island as it takes shape.

item.content:encoded:
Jam update: Sat 6:17 PM

Saturday, November 14, 2026 at 6:17 PM Central

Saturday afternoon: a controller run, a falling light, and a button that drew the wrong picture

At 3 PM the owner sat down with a PlayStation 5 pad and played the island for about eight minutes. Nobody else's hands were on it. It was the first run where the new quick-time moment, the falling stage light, was on screen for a real player, and it showed us what a pad run is for.

What worked, seen in the recording: when the light starts to fall, a ring and a button picture appear over the actor. Tapping the asked button three times saved the show, and the sheet paid out "+$100 saved the show". The diner came up for every show, and the genre chose the world around it: a forest for Horror, then a jungle for Sci-Fi, each loaded in about three seconds.

What he hit:

  • A button that drew the wrong picture. Any "press as it closes" moment showed a different button than the one it wanted, so it could not be won. The cause was a widget that quietly switches its own pictures back on whenever the controller layout refreshes. Each picture now sits in its own box, and it is the box that hides.
  • The wrong button did not count. Circle never reached the game as the button it was asked to be.
  • The wrap sheet closed in the second it opened, because the presses from the last moment were still arriving. Very short takes had the same cause: a second press right after Action cut the take.
  • The grey "Talk (hold)" card was still there during takes and over the menu.
  • A Horror opening that never spoke. In all five Horror shows in the logs, the Showrunner's opening line stayed silent while other genres spoke. We do not know why yet; the next change tries plainer wording, and it is switched off until someone plays it.

What was fixed by 3:38, with an honest label on each. All of these are in the build now, and none has been played again yet:

  • The quick-time moment takes over the buttons while it is up and for two seconds after, so a mashed press can no longer cut the take or close the sheet.
  • Circle now answers it, and the moment asks only for Triangle, Square or Circle.
  • The picture fix described above.
  • The talk card stays hidden over menus and between takes, and comes back only for a real conversation.
  • The Showrunner waits 22 seconds, not 10, before her opening is sent again; a first line takes up to 16 seconds to start, and each resend was restarting her.
  • The interview camera sits further back and higher, so her office shows around her. The frame above, from before the change, is a face and a wall.
  • The first take of an episode now holds a three-second wide shot of the set before anyone speaks, and in the interview you can pick someone to talk to before the first take.
  • The props library grew from 71 to 94 props.

The second picture shows the other way a moment can end: the show cancelled, "The light came down, CUT!". That is the game doing what it should. It was the wrong picture that made it unfair, and that is what we spent the afternoon on.

item.content:encoded:
Jam update: Sat 12:17 PM

Saturday, November 14, 2026 at 12:17 PM Central

Saturday, noon: first controller playtest, and one diner in two worlds

Until this morning every full take had been played with a mouse and keyboard. Late this morning the game was played start to finish on a controller for the first time, two whole shows. Most of it held up. Two things did not, and both are ones a player would meet in the first minute.

The first is a talk prompt. Fortnite's own "Talk (hold)" card for an actor stayed on the screen the whole time, menus included, where holding the button does nothing. The cause was ours: the game was pointing the player at an actor after every take instead of only while the director is giving notes. A change that points the player at an actor only during notes has been written. It has not been played yet.

The second is the wrap sheet at the end of a take. On the controller only one of its four buttons ever took a press. Looking inside the sheet turned up one real difference: the three buttons that failed each carry a small button icon, and that icon was catching mouse clicks meant for the button under it. The icons have been made click-through. Whether that also cures the controller we do not know yet; it may be a separate fault, and we are reading the logs from that session to find out. None of this counts as fixed until it is played on a controller again.

The bigger change today is that sets and biomes are being pulled apart. A set is the building and the marks the cameras use; a biome is the world around it. The goal is one diner that can stand in a desert or a forest, and later a city or a jungle. The two pictures below are views from the editor, not from a take: the same diner, with the desert around it and then the forest. The open water at the edges is the next thing to hide. It has not been seen in play yet, and a mistake in how the diner was tied to its desert was caught an hour ago, before anyone played it.

This morning a random Director's Challenge was added too. At Action, each full take draws one goal, such as getting an actor to tell a joke, and pays a bonus if it happens. It is in the build and has not been played, so we cannot say how it feels.

2 more are in progress. The team pushed 58 project updates across Verse gameplay code, art, props and materials, audio.

item.content:encoded:
Jam update: Sat 6:17 AM

Saturday, November 14, 2026 at 6:17 AM Central

Saturday, 6:00 AM: one take, read like a film strip

Dev log entry for Saturday November 14, 2026, at six in the morning. Every picture marked "from the game" is a real take played overnight.

At midnight the camera in our castle set was looking at the back of a wall. This is the same set six hours later, one frame for each line of an eight-line scene, in order:

The speaker is in the picture in all eight frames, with a face you can read in seven. No walls. One back of a head. We have been keeping that count all night, because "it looks better" is not a measurement:

  • 2 AM, three sets: no speaker's face in any frame, and the camera on the wrong actor five times in nine.
  • 4 AM, the castle: speaker in frame four times in eight, a bare wall once.
  • 5 AM: six in eight.
  • 6 AM: eight in eight.

Three things got it there, and none of them was clever. The standing spots the cameras could not see were found by measuring every one of them and moved a few steps. The camera was stopped from cutting away to the listener more than twice a take. And the actors now turn slightly toward the audience when they talk to each other, as stage actors always have.

The same playing turned up a mistake that had been in front of us for hours: the character cast as the ghoul had been walking around in someone else's costume, a hooded figure in red and black. The casting was fine; one entry in her costume record pointed at the wrong character. She is herself again in the strip above.

The space station was played for the first time tonight too. Its windows look onto a field of stars, and when the scene turns dangerous the whole bridge goes red for eight seconds.

What still is not right as the sun comes up: a second show in the same sitting does not start by itself, one actor wandered off the set mid-scene, and nobody has yet played a full show with a controller in their hands. Today is for those, and for the people who make this game to wake up and play it.

item.content:encoded:
Jam update: Sat 3:17 AM

Saturday, November 14, 2026 at 3:17 AM Central

Saturday, 3:00 AM: the camera learns to look at the person talking

Dev log entry for Saturday November 14, 2026, written at three in the morning. Pictures marked "from the game" are real takes played tonight.

Two hours ago we opened every set like a stage so the cameras could see in. Then we did the only thing that proves anything: we played it, set after set, and wrote down what each frame actually showed.

The first pass was humbling. Four sets, sixteen lines of dialogue, and a simple count: a blank wall in the picture, zero times. That was the fix working. The speaker's face in the picture: also zero times. The camera no longer hid behind walls, but it was framing chests and elbows, and five times out of nine it was pointed at the actor who was listening.

So the camera got three new rules before the next pass. Show the one who is speaking. Aim at the face, not the middle of the body. And never choose a shot you have not checked. We played the same three sets again with the same cast.

The second count: wrong actor, none. Shots with nothing usable in them, none, where there had been nine. One true close-up of a speaking face, one two-shot worth keeping. That is not finished. Heads still get cut off when the camera lands beside an actor, and the western town's wide shot makes its cast look like ants. But it is the first time tonight the game looked like someone was directing it.

Horror turned out to have its own problem: darkness. Measured from the frames, a horror scene was about a seventh as bright as a daylight one. We did not want to wash the mood out, so the rule we settled on has two halves: a wide shot must always be bright enough to read, and a close-up may stay as dark as it likes so long as a face or a pair of eyes comes through. Each actor now carries a stronger light in dark scenes, and a follow spot finds whoever is speaking.

The other thing seen in the game for the first time tonight is the end of a take. It used to stop on a plain cut screen. Now the curtain comes down on a sheet that says "That's a wrap": what the take made at the box office, what the cast, the location and the film cost, how many stars it earned, a one-line tip, and your director level.

That sheet also taught us the night's most useful lesson. It trapped our tester: no click and no key would close it. The cause was a single unticked setting that says whether a panel is allowed to take focus. With it off, every instruction to focus the panel was ignored without a word of complaint. The same setting explains why nothing had ever answered a controller. It is ticked now, and written into our rules.

Elsewhere tonight: the director's office, where every show starts, went from a concrete yard to a room with posters, trophies and a film camera; the count of hand props we have modelled reached seventy-one, each with its own icon; and the space station got a red alert.

Still not done at three o'clock: nobody has seen a prop in an actor's hand, wide shots at night are too dark, and no one has yet played a full show with a controller. Those are next.

item.content:encoded:
Jam update: Sat 1:29 AM

Saturday, November 14, 2026 at 1:29 AM Central

Saturday, 1:30 AM: the night we opened every set

Dev log entry for Saturday November 14, 2026. Written overnight. Pictures are from the editor unless a caption says they are from the game.

The last thing we were told before the studio went to sleep was blunt: most of the time you cannot see the show. The camera sits behind a wall, or looks at the back of a prop, while two AI actors perform a scene nobody can watch. For a game about directing a show, that is the one fault that cannot ship.

So tonight we stopped fixing blocked shots one playtest at a time and measured all of them. A script stands a figure on every spot an actor can use, on every set, and from each spot tries every camera position the game is able to choose: the wide shot, close-ups, over-the-shoulder, pans, dollies, the crane. For each one it asks a simple question: is anything between the lens and this actor's face?

The first numbers were hard to read. In the castle, 30 camera lines in 100 reached an actor. In the old theatre, 40. In the jungle temple, 48. The widest shot, the one meant to show the whole scene, was blocked every single time on all three.

The cause turned out to be simple. Our cameras stand six to fourteen metres back, and the rooms are smaller than that. The lens was outside the building.

The fix is the oldest trick in film and television: a set is not a room, it is a stage with one wall missing. We opened every set on the side where the cameras work. Outer walls came off, a bay window and a tower roof left the castle, partitions and a vending machine left the theatre, a barn lost half its west wall. Each set also got a marker that says "the audience sits here", and no camera is allowed to stand further back than it.

By a quarter past one, all eight sets measured between 90 and 99 clear lines in 100. The game's own camera code changed too: every shot now checks that it can see its actor before it is used, and picks a different shot if it cannot.

Then we played it, and the game reminded us that a measurement is not a show. In the first take on the western town, every shot was rejected and replaced, because one actor was sitting in a chair that no camera could see, and our new rule insisted on seeing everyone. The picture below is from the build before tonight's changes, and it is exactly the complaint we started with: the director's panel is up, and behind it the camera is staring at a porch rail.

That chair has been moved and the rule corrected. The same shot gets taken again on the next build, and we will post it either way.

Other things that moved tonight:

  • Money. A take now costs something: rent for the location, film for every take, and the cast's day rates. It earns box office, a score in stars, and progress toward the next director level. The first take played on the new rules made $420, cost $350, and earned one star with the advice "more emotions".
  • Props. Forty-five hand props of our own are modelled, with twenty-four new short animations for holding and using them. No actor has held one in the game yet; that test is running as this is written.
  • The game played itself, almost. For the first time one of our AI helpers drove the whole game by mouse, from the title screen through casting, the set, the genre and a full eight-line take to the final CUT, and then filed a list of everything that was wrong with the menus on the way.

What is honest to say at half past one: the sets are open, the numbers are good, the code is in, and none of it has yet been watched working in a full take with the actors in every frame. That is what the rest of the night is for.

We're deep into the weekend with about 42 hours still on the clock, and the team has been busy with 87 updates across gameplay code, art, props, materials, and audio. Right now we're doing a big sight-line audit, checking every camera position against every set and then opening things up by pulling out walls and reworking layouts so the action is easy to see. No big milestones to announce just yet, but plenty of polish is landing behind the scenes. Stay tuned for visuals soon!

In progress

  • Sight-line audit: trace every camera position against every set, then open the sets (walls out, layouts changed)
